headline: Cape May Rips: Bluefish Steady, Bay Fluke Tucked Tight, Drum Run a Distant Memory
subhead: The rips are giving up honest bluefish on the tide change, the bay's holding weakfish and croaker in the channels, and if you're still hunting drum you're two months late.
body_markdown:
Rips grade: fair. Not the kind of fair where I'm apologizing for it — fair like an honest B-minus. You work the tide right off Cape May Point, you eat. You show up whenever and drift wherever, you're chumming for nothing.

Here's why. The current through the Rips is still running hard on the ebb, especially that two-hour window before dead low when the outflow from the bay meets the ocean swell and everything gets churned up and confused — that's when the bait gets disoriented and the blues pile on it. I've been running bunker chunks on fishfinder rigs, 20 to 40 feet, right where that seam sets up between the Point and the shoal, and it's been a hook-up an hour, sometimes better. Size has been decent too — 3 to 4 pound blues mixed with a few pushing 6, not the snapper-class stuff you're pulling out of the back bays. Stripers on the ocean side? Forget it for now. That's a fall story. Anybody telling you different in mid-August is selling you something.

Hereford Inlet's been the more interesting story, honestly. Snapper blues are thick as fleas in there — Grassy Sound, the back channels behind Wildwood Crest, anywhere there's current pushing bait past a piling. We flagged a couple weeks back that those snappers were a sign the adult class would keep building through late August into September, and that's exactly the shape it's taking. Still mostly the small stuff right now, but I'm seeing more 2 and 3 pounders mixed in on the last of the outgoing than I was two weeks ago. Give it another couple weeks and that back bay bluefish bite is going to have some shoulders on it.

Fluke inside the inlet have been a mixed bag — plenty of shorts, a keeper here and there for guys working 4-inch Gulp swimming mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails tight to the bulkheads and the inlet's deeper holes on the last two hours of the outgoing. The water's warm enough now that these fish are lazy — they want the bait dragged slow right past their nose, not worked hard. Same story I told you two weeks ago and it's held: with the bay running warm on the surface, the bait's staying tight to structure, and that's exactly where the fluke and weakfish have parked themselves. We called that one and it's still playing out.

Speaking of the bay — if you're asking me about drum, I've got bad news. That run's done. Fortescue, the Cohansey mouth, the Ship John area — that whole show wrapped up back in May like it does every year, and there is nothing sniffing a clam down there right now worth your gas money. Anybody still hunting drum in August either doesn't fish the Delaware or is hoping I'll tell them something I can't. I won't sugarcoat that one.

What the bay's actually giving up right now is weakfish and croaker, and they're holding deep — the channels off Fortescue and down toward the mouth, 20 to 35 feet, not up on the flats where the water's baking into the mid-70s and climbing. Bloodworms and Fishbites on bottom rigs, or if you want to work for it, a bucktail tipped with squid strip dragged slow along the channel edges on the tail end of the flood. Kingfish and spot are showing on the lower bay flats too, which tells you the classic late-summer Delaware pattern is setting up right on schedule — that's your croaker season building, and it typically peaks over the next couple weeks as the water holds warm.

The recent rain out of Jersey pushed a good slug of fresh water down through the upper bay, and that's staining things up around the Maurice River and upper Cohansey pretty good. If you fished up there this week and got nothing, that's why — the cleaner water and the fish that go with it have shifted down toward the lower bay and the ocean-side inlets. I'd stay south of Fortescue right now if you want water with some color to it instead of chocolate milk.

For keeper sea bass and better fluke, I'm sending guys offshore to the reef sites — the Del wrecks and Old Grounds have been the more consistent play while the bay itself goes soft and warm for anything with real teeth in it. Triggerfish have been mixed in around that same structure too, which is about right for this time of year — they like the warm water and they'll hang on the wrecks right alongside the sea bass.

Looking ahead, I don't expect much to change fast. The bay's going to keep running warm through the rest of August, which means weakfish and croaker stay deep in the channels and the fluke stay glued to structure rather than roaming the flats. If we get a stretch of northwest wind to knock that surface heat down a couple degrees, I'd expect the flats bite to open back up some. Until then, work the deep water, work the tide change at the Rips, and don't waste a trip looking for drum that left in the spring.
